strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuine, previously under-addressed problem in class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrariness of learned canonical poses, which prevents meaningful cross-instance comparison of relative pose/symmetry distributions.

Provides a principled, proof-backed solution (Proposition 3.1 / Appendix B) showing that normalizing by the empirical Fréchet mean of relative transformations recovers an identity-centered approximation of the true symmetry distribution, with convergence guarantees in Wasserstein distance.

Extends symmetry discovery beyond the common 2D/SO(2) image setting to large-scale, real molecular conformation data (GEOM/QM9) under SO(3), which the authors claim (and appear) to be a first for this class of unsupervised symmetry-discovery methods.

Demonstrates several qualitatively compelling results: data-aligned canonical poses (upright digits), correct disambiguation of partial symmetries (distinguishing 6 vs 9 despite shared 180°-relation), and a practical downstream application (out-of-distribution pose detection) with reasonable AUC-ROC scores.
Reasonably thorough appendix with architecture and training details (encoder/decoder specifics, hyperparameters, loss weighting, hardware) that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Quantitative comparisons against baselines (SGM, IE-AE, or other learned-symmetry methods such as Augerino/partial G-CNNs/VP G-CNNs) are largely qualitative (side-by-side figures) rather than systematic quantitative benchmarks with shared metrics, making it hard to judge the magnitude of improvement RECON provides over prior class-pose decomposition or symmetry-discovery methods.

The GEOM experiment's "ground-truth" SO(3) symmetries are synthetically imposed via matrix-Fisher sampling rather than being intrinsic/known symmetries of the molecules, which weakens the claim of validating on "real-world" symmetry distributions; it is closer to a semi-synthetic benchmark.

Sensitivity/ablation analysis (e.g., effect of neighborhood size k, choice of parametric family for the recovered distribution, robustness to seed/initialization) is only shown for the MNIST experiment and not extended to the more complex GEOM/SO(3) setting.

The overall pipeline is fairly complex (train IE-AE backbone, perform k-NN-based canonical normalization, then separately train Θ and Λ predictors from pseudo-labels), and the paper offers limited analysis of failure propagation across these stages or robustness to backbone quality/pretraining choices.

Absolute error metrics reported (e.g., MSE thresholds, AUC-ROC values) lack strong context from competitive baselines, making it difficult to assess how good these numbers really are relative to alternative unsupervised symmetry discovery approaches.

The method still requires the transformation group G to be specified a priori, and the discussion of limitations (self-symmetric ambiguities, need for richer density families) suggests the approach may be fragile in more complex or multimodal symmetry regimes beyond the tested cases.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: unsupervised discovery of instance-specific symmetry distributions, resolving the arbitrary-canonical-pose ambiguity inherent to class-pose decomposition methods (IE-AE, SGM, etc.).

Provides a principled theoretical foundation (Proposition 3.1) grounded in Fréchet means and Wasserstein-distance convergence, with a full proof in the appendix, giving the normalization procedure a rigorous justification rather than being purely heuristic.

First demonstration of symmetry discovery extended to 3D SO(3) transformations on a large, real-world dataset (GEOM/QM9 molecular conformations), going beyond the typical 2D image benchmarks used in prior symmetry-discovery work.

Nice qualitative result showing the method can distinguish visually related but semantically distinct classes (e.g., digits '6' and '9') that standard fully-equivariant methods conflate, illustrating a genuine advantage of instance-specific, class-conditioned normalization.
Useful downstream application (OOD pose detection) with quantitative AUC-ROC results across three datasets, showing a concrete practical use of the learned distributions.
Extensive implementation/reproducibility details in the appendix (architectures, hyperparameters, training schedules) and a stated commitment to public code release.
weaknesses: Quantitative comparisons to the most relevant baselines (SGM, plain IE-AE without normalization) are largely qualitative/visual (e.g., Figures 4-6b) rather than reported as direct numeric metrics (e.g., Wasserstein distance or MAE of recovered distribution vs. ground truth) side-by-side with RECON, weakening the empirical case for improvement over prior methods.

The equivalence class [x] is approximated via k-NN in the invariant latent space rather than the connected-component definition used in the theory; sensitivity to k is only studied for MNIST, leaving open how robust the 3D/molecular results are to this approximation.

Ground-truth symmetries in all experiments (MNIST, FashionMNIST, GEOM) are synthetically injected by the authors themselves rather than being naturally occurring, which is reasonable for controlled evaluation but somewhat limits evidence that RECON recovers genuinely intrinsic, real-world symmetries as opposed to recovering an artificially imposed distribution it was implicitly designed to match.

The parametric assumptions used for pseudo-labels and the Θ/Λ predictors (uniform/Gaussian for 2D, unimodal matrix-Fisher for 3D) are restrictive; the paper acknowledges in the limitations that multi-modal or self-symmetric distributions are not well handled, but this is not empirically stress-tested.

Error analysis on GEOM (about 20% of molecules with high MSE) is somewhat underexplored — the paper does not isolate the actual causes (conformer sampling limits vs. mixed symmetries vs. backbone capacity) beyond speculation.

No discussion of computational overhead/scalability of the extra normalization and learnable-mapping training stages relative to baseline class-pose decomposition training, which is relevant given the added training phases (IE-AE + normalization + Θ/Λ training) for practical adoption.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine, underappreciated problem in class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrariness of learned canonical poses, which obscures interpretability and downstream usability of relative-pose distributions.

Provides theoretical grounding (Proposition 3.1 with a full proof) showing that right-multiplying by the empirical Fréchet mean of relative poses approximates the true identity-centered symmetry distribution, plus a principled robust extension (Tukey-Fréchet mean) for multimodal cases.

First demonstration of instance-specific symmetry discovery extended to 3D (SO(3)) on a large, real molecular dataset (GEOM-QM9), going beyond the typical 2D-only scope of prior symmetry-discovery work.

Two practical, architecture-agnostic downstream applications (OOD pose detection and training-free test-time canonicalization for frozen pretrained backbones) that are compelling and broadly useful if they generalize.

Extensive supplementary material: ablations on neighborhood size, equivalence-class quality (hit-rate) validation, detailed implementation and training details, and comparisons across multiple estimators/backbones.
Qualitatively interesting result on partial symmetries (distinguishing rotated '6' vs '9') that other class-pose/canonicalization methods reportedly fail to capture.
weaknesses: Quantitative comparisons are largely limited to the same IE-AE backbone with/without RECON normalization; more recent/competing symmetry-discovery methods (SGM, VP G-CNN, WSCNN) are discussed only qualitatively or in passing rather than benchmarked head-to-head on the core discovery, OOD, or canonicalization tasks.

Main image experiments (MNIST/FashionMNIST) use synthetically imposed, class-conditioned rotation ranges rather than naturally occurring instance-specific symmetries, which somewhat limits the realism of the validation despite being a reasonable controlled testbed.

The method's success is contingent on the invariant latent space Z producing well-separated, connected clusters for k-NN-based class approximation; while a hit-rate metric is reported for GEOM, this dependency could be fragile in less well-behaved or more complex real-world data (acknowledged as a limitation for multi-object/natural images).
Code is not available at submission time (promised only upon publication), limiting independent verification during review.
Results are often reported as single point estimates (e.g., Fig. 5a, Fig. 6d) without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, making it harder to assess statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The contribution is essentially a post-hoc normalization/correction step layered on an existing architecture (IE-AE) rather than a fundamentally new representation-learning method, which, combined with limited baseline comparisons, somewhat tempers the significance of the technical contribution.

strengths: Provides a clear, well-motivated theoretical contribution (Proposition 3.1) with a full proof in the appendix, showing that the Fréchet mean of relative poses can be used to correct for arbitrary canonical offsets in class-pose decomposition methods.

The method is simple (a right-multiplication by the inverse empirical Fréchet mean), architecture-agnostic, and requires no retraining of the underlying class-pose backbone, which is an attractive practical property.

First demonstration of instance-specific symmetry discovery extended to 3D groups (SO(3)) using large-scale, real molecular conformation data (GEOM-QM9), going beyond the 2D-only scope of prior work (SGM, WSCNN, Partial G-CNN, VP G-CNN).

Introduces a robust Tukey-Fréchet mean variant to handle multimodal symmetry distributions where the classical Fréchet mean can fall outside the distribution's support, with supporting simulations in Appendix C.

Demonstrates a practically useful downstream application: test-time canonicalization that grants approximate group invariance to frozen, pre-trained classifiers without retraining, with sizable accuracy gains over both uncanonicalized and arbitrarily-canonicalized (IE-AE) baselines across MNIST, FashionMNIST, and GEOM-QM9.

Shows a nice qualitative advantage in handling partial symmetries (e.g., distinguishing 6 vs 9 related by 180° rotation), which fully-equivariant and existing class-pose methods (IE-AE, SGM) collapse into the same canonical.

Reasonably thorough ablations and diagnostics in the appendix (neighborhood size sensitivity, equivalence-class hit-rate quality, error vs. molecule attributes) that support the robustness of the proposed pipeline.

Good positioning relative to a substantial body of related work on learning symmetries from data and class-pose decomposition methods, clarifying the method's novelty relative to closely related approaches like SGM.
weaknesses: All main experiments are built exclusively on the IE-AE backbone; despite claims that RECON is compatible with other class-pose methods (SGM, Quotient Autoencoders, Marchetti et al.), no experiments validate this generality, leaving the broader applicability claim untested.

Main quantitative results (Fig. 5a, Fig. 5c AUC-ROC table, Fig. 6d test-time canonicalization table) appear to be reported from single runs without error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness/variance of the reported improvements.

The OOD detection and test-time canonicalization experiments only compare RECON against the uncentered IE-AE baseline; no empirical comparison is made against SGM (identified as the most closely related method) or against frame-averaging/other invariance-granting baselines that are discussed only qualitatively.

The acknowledged limitation that class-pose decomposition (and thus RECON) operates at the instance/whole-input level rather than object level significantly restricts applicability to natural, multi-object real-world images, which is a substantial scope limitation for claims of general applicability.

Symmetry ground truths in all experiments are synthetically imposed (rotations sampled from known parametric distributions per class), so the evaluation, while useful for validation, does not demonstrate discovery of genuinely unknown, naturally-occurring symmetries in the wild.

The framework is only empirically validated for rotation groups SO(2)/SO(3); despite being presented as general to Lie groups G, no experiments explore other transformation groups (e.g., scaling, general affine, or non-rotation Lie groups) to substantiate this generality.

The paper is notation-heavy and dense, which, combined with substantial reliance on appendix material for core experimental and proof details, may reduce accessibility and complicate independent verification without the (currently unavailable) code release.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and clearly-articulated problem: arbitrary canonical poses in class-pose decomposition methods obscure the shared symmetry structure across instances of the same class, and the proposed right-translation correction (Prop 3.1) is a simple, elegant, and theoretically grounded fix (with a Wasserstein convergence proof).
The Tukey-Fréchet robust mean extension is a thoughtful addition that addresses a real failure mode (multimodal distributions) of the naive Fréchet mean, with clear illustrative examples (Fig. 4, 8).

Empirical validation spans both 2D image data (MNIST/FashionMNIST with class-dependent synthetic rotation distributions) and a large-scale, realistic 3D molecular conformer dataset (GEOM-QM9), which is beyond the 2D-only scope of most prior symmetry-discovery work.

Two practical downstream applications (OOD pose detection and plug-and-play test-time canonicalization for frozen pretrained backbones) are demonstrated, with the latter showing consistent, sometimes large, improvements over baselines (e.g., outperforming Partial G-CNNs and matching/exceeding some fully equivariant architectures on FashionMNIST).

Extensive appendix material: hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (k-NN size), qualitative/quantitative diagnostics of the equivalence-class definition (hit-rate analysis), computational overhead reporting, and thorough implementation details support reproducibility and transparency about limitations.
Honest discussion of limitations (instance-level vs. object-level decomposition, reliance on class-pose backbones, k-NN approximation) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The core empirical validation of symmetry recovery relies on synthetic ground-truth symmetries manually imposed on the data (rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST, matrix-Fisher-augmented GEOM-QM9); there is little demonstration on data where symmetries are naturally present and unknown, which is the actual motivating use case of the paper.

The comparison to SGM (Allingham et al., 2024), described as the most closely related method, is largely qualitative (Fig. 2) rather than a rigorous quantitative comparison on the same symmetry-discovery/downstream benchmarks; a direct head-to-head with SGM would strengthen the claims of improvement.

The method's dependence on the k-NN heuristic for approximating equivalence classes |x| is a practical weak point: performance is sensitive to class overlap (as shown in the FashionMNIST failure analysis), and the paper acknowledges but does not solve this limitation, relegating mitigation strategies to future work.

The test-time canonicalization results, while positive, show a meaningful accuracy gap relative to specialized equivariant architectures on MNIST (90.96% vs 94.72%), and the FashionMNIST 'win' relies on the fully-equivariant SE(2) ESCNN baseline underperforming rather than RECON being close to an accuracy ceiling; the practical significance is somewhat data-dependent.

The instance-level (not object-centric) formulation, acknowledged as a limitation, restricts applicability to well-controlled, single-object-per-image or single-molecule settings, limiting significance for more realistic multi-object scenes; no experiments address this gap.

Several hyperparameters and design choices (k for each dataset, robustness parameter c for Tukey-Fréchet, group G assumed known a priori) reduce the 'unsupervised discovery' framing, since domain knowledge and tuning are still required.

The GEOM-QM9 evaluation assumes the correct group (SO(3)) and parametric family (matrix-Fisher) are known in advance; the claim of 'discovering' symmetries is therefore more about estimating parameters of a presumed distribution family than fully non-parametric discovery, somewhat overstating the generality claimed in the abstract/intro.
